en: I now added
many more skills here. You of course find
them all attached.
And one of these skills,
my
React Best Practices skill, also has a
references subfolder because that is
something you can do.
Your skills can just be a skill.md file. And
frankly, for me, most of my skills are, but
if you have extra documentation, that may
belong to a skill, but that doesn't always
matter when a skill is loaded, then you can
put that in extra files, which should be
stored in a references folder.
Like here in this React Best Practices
skill, in there I have some general rules on
how I would like my React code to be
written.
But there is then one rule in there or one
point where I tell it to avoid using
useEffect, which is a React feature, doesn't
matter for this course. The thing just is I
have an entire detailed document here with
more details on how to avoid useEffect and
when to avoid it. Now, this is pretty long
and I don't want to load that into every
context every time this React skill gets
used because of course, yes, this skill is
loaded lazily, not all the time, but this is
a React project in the end. Most of my code
here is related to React. So this skill may
be loaded quite a bit and I don't always
want to load this huge document. Instead,
that should be loaded only when the agent is
working on user fact-related code. And
that's the idea. This will not be loaded
automatically, this extra document. Instead,
the agent is just made aware of it and it
can then also load this extra document
lazily if it needs it. So you can build
skills that can grow incrementally so where
the agent can discover more and more parts
as they need it.
And that's therefore another very useful
pattern to be aware of. Another example for
a skill
is this SQLite Explorer skill. This one
comes with a script.
This script is all about giving access to my
SQLite database using Bun. So it in the end
exposes a little tool, you could say,
that allows
us or the AI to run queries against the
database. In the skill.md file, I therefore
have the name of the skill, a description
that describes it, and then some rules on
how to use this skill and ultimately the
script therefore, and then I point at that
script. I tell it that it can be found in
the scripts folder and what the name is and
how to run that script. I use this
placeholder here to increase the chances of
the AI finding the script because in my
experience that is sometimes a bit shaky and
it doesn't correctly find the script.
But with that we can of course use the skill
like any other skill.
We can check that it's available. Here it
is.
And then we could ask the AI to list all
users in our database. That may be enough to
automatically invoke the skill, but again,
we don't have to hope. We can just
explicitly invoke it and send this off to
the AI.
And this will now load that skill.
The AI then also lists the scripts and it
executes my script here with various inputs
and then returns the requested data, which
could of course, for example, be useful for
debugging my app or getting more information
about the current state and which most
importantly gives the AI a safe way of
looking into the database.
And that's just one of many examples on how
you could use skills.
